sections.report:
Walk (working notes):

First read: the eye lands on the bold sans headline "Notes for ferry passengers" (top left, around y 65–105) and then drops into four serif paragraphs. It reads as a plain information page for people using a river ferry. It feels calm, and it reads like a document more than a notice.

The whole piece:
- Can a first-time viewer say in one sentence what this is for? yes
- Do image and headline make one idea? yes (there's no image, so there's nothing to clash)
- Does every element do a job? yes (only a heading and paragraphs. The first-line indents used together with space between paragraphs belong to the Text section)
- Do type, colours and shapes share one mood and era? yes (a sans heading over serif body text is a coherent, current pairing)
- Is the copy finished? yes (no placeholder text and no typos)
- Does each kind of element look the same everywhere? yes (all four paragraphs share one treatment)
- Do colours, shapes and directions carry the right mood? yes (quiet and neutral, which suits practical notes)
- Does each heading name what its section holds? yes

No line was answered no or unsure, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

One copy note that no checklist line covers. The director can rank it or drop it. The times a passenger would act on are vague. "Between early morning and late evening" (para 1, y≈176) and "the last crossing leaves the quay before dusk" (para 3, y≈444) don't give a clock time. Someone planning a winter return trip can't tell when the last boat goes, and "before dusk" could mean any time in roughly the last hour of daylight. If they read it as too late, they miss the boat. Fix: give the first and last departure times for each season, or say plainly that the posted timetable is the authority. Kind: defect. Weight: minor for a general notes page, major if this page is where passengers check times.

**What's working.**
- The headline names exactly what the page holds and who it's for, so a passenger knows in a second that it's meant for them and what kind of thing it is.
- The piece is one consistent thing. There's one heading style, one paragraph style and a single ink colour on white, with no decoration competing with the text, which suits a practical notice.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye lands at once on the bold sans heading "Notes for ferry passengers" (about x 120–593, y 68–105). It then drops into four indented serif paragraphs of equal weight, read from top to bottom. It reads as a plain information note for ferry riders, and it feels calm and quiet. The image is about one screen (about 1280×800), so I judged it from the whole image. I assume the job is to give passengers practical facts about the ferry: times, bicycles, the winter timetable and the landings.

What matters first:
- Does one element stand clearly above the rest? **Yes.** The heading is the only bold, the only sans and the largest text.
- Can you tell each level of the text from the next at a glance? **Yes.** There are only two levels, title and body, and their sizes are far apart. No two sizes are close.
- Do the headings differ from the text in more than size? **Yes.** The title is a bold sans and the body is a regular serif.

No line was answered `no` or `unsure`, so I did not need to open any entries.

---

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

(Not on this checklist, for the director to weigh: under the title, all four paragraphs carry the same weight. A passenger looking for one fact, such as the last winter crossing or the bicycle rules, has to read the prose to find it. No subheads or lead words mark the topics. This is a scanning question rather than a hierarchy defect. It is taste/common sense, minor.)

**What's working.**
- The title stands out in three ways at once: size, weight, and sans set against serif. That makes it the clear entry point without any extra decoration, and it matches the "bolder, not bigger" idea in Refactoring UI.
- There are only two levels and they are far apart, so no size reads as a near-miss. For a short note like this, a third level isn't needed.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No. All the content sits in the upper left: one text column from x≈120 to x≈770, and from y≈65 to y≈560. The right ~510 px (x≈770–1280) is blank for the full height, and so is the bottom ~240 px. Nothing on the right acts as a counterweight. The viewer meets a page that looks pushed into one corner, more like a page that did not finish loading or a missing sidebar than a chosen layout. The column itself reads fine. Arnheim (*Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance") says a heavy side needs a counterweight. On a reading page, a left-set column with open space beside it is a common and acceptable pattern, so this is not about whether the text can be read. It is about whether the empty half looks meant. Fix direction: make the open area look deliberate. Either put the column in a frame that owns the space (center the measure, or set a wider left margin so the column sits nearer the middle), or put something light but useful in the right column, such as the next-departure time, a small map, or the landing addresses. Taste, with Arnheim's balance principle behind it. Weight: minor. The notes are still read top to bottom without trouble.

**What's working.**
- One clean column with a single shared left edge at x≈120 for both the heading and the body. There are no near-misses, so the page reads as one ordered block, and the eye moves straight from the heading down through the four paragraphs.
- The heading sits close to its text. The gap is about 33 px, about the same as the gaps between paragraphs, and the heading's size and weight carry the rest. It clearly belongs to the column below it and does not float above it.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (visual weight balances)

**Section.** Text: applies. This is a one-column reading page: a sans-serif bold heading over four serif body paragraphs.

**Findings**
1. **"Are paragraphs marked by an indent or by space, never both, with the first paragraph after a heading flush left?"** No. All four paragraphs start with a deep indent of about 47 px (x≈120→167, roughly 2.5 em at this size). They are also separated by about 20 px of extra space beyond the normal line spacing (for example, "boat." at y≈233 and "Bicycles" at y≈281, where lines are about 29 px apart). The first paragraph, right under the heading at y≈147, is indented too. The reader gets the same "new paragraph" signal twice. The indent under the heading leaves a notch at the top-left corner of the text block, so the block doesn't sit cleanly under the heading's left edge. The page looks set by default rather than by intent, and the deep indent makes the left edge look ragged when the gaps already separate the paragraphs. Bringhurst (*Elements of Typographic Style*) and Butterick (*Practical Typography*) both say to use one marker, not two, and to set the first paragraph after a heading flush. Fix: on a short web page like this, keep the space between paragraphs and remove the indents. If you'd rather keep indents, close the gaps, reduce the indent to about 1 em, and set the first paragraph flush left. **Convention.** Weight: **minor**. It's a craft flaw, and it doesn't stop anyone reading the notes.

**What's working.**
- **Comfortable measure and line spacing.** Body lines run about 60–72 characters (for example, "crossing takes about twelve minutes in calm weather, and a little longer"). The line spacing looks like about 1.5 at roughly 19 px type. That's in Bringhurst's 45–75 range, and the eye moves easily from the end of one line to the start of the next.
- **Two faces in clear contrast.** The bold sans heading and the serif body are plainly different, each has one job, and neither nearly matches the other. The body is set in a plain reading serif in dark grey on white, so contrast is clearly sufficient.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (paragraphs marked by indent or space, not both)

I didn't open the reference entry for the one failing line or run the crop script, because Bash access was denied. The finding is based on the rule as I know it from those two books, and the measurements are estimated by eye from the full image (about 1280×800 px).

sections.report:
**First read:** The eye goes to the bold sans heading "Notes for ferry passengers" at the top left, then down into four serif paragraphs. It's a plain, calm information page for ferry riders. Everything is near-black on white, with no hue anywhere.

**What it's for (assumed):** a short web notice that gives ferry passengers practical facts.

**Walk, Color section:**
- Small palette: yes. It uses only one neutral range, near-black on white.
- Strong colour kept to a small share of the area: yes. There is no saturated colour.
- Clear range of light and dark: yes. Dark text on white has full value contrast and reads the same in grayscale.
- Warm forward, cool receding: yes. There are no temperatures in play.
- Matching colours look the same: yes. The heading and body text are the same near-black throughout.
- No vibrating edges: yes. There are no neighbouring strong colours.
- Status colours used for their usual meaning: yes. There are none.
- Meaning not carried by colour alone: yes. Nothing is encoded in colour.
- Dark theme not pure black: yes. The page is light-themed, so this doesn't apply.

No line is answered no or unsure, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies. The page uses only neutral colour: near-black text on a white page.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** The palette is one neutral range: a soft near-black (not pure #000) on white for both the heading (x≈120–595, y≈65–105) and the body text (x≈120–770, y≈135–560). That gives full value contrast for long reading without the harshness of pure black on white. The heading stands out by weight and typeface, not by colour, so nothing competes with the text and the page stays calm.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The image is a text-only page: a heading and four paragraphs on white. It has no photo, illustration, icon, logo, mark, broken-image icon or empty placeholder box. The blank area on the right (about x 790–1280) is just empty space, with no frame marking where an image should go.

**Findings**
None.
